about: The two fixed practice exams in the May 2027 format (docs/aphug-architecture.md, "Practice exams"): Section I is 60 five-option questions in course order, one block a standalone question or a whole stimulus set; a bank question's fifth option is in the form's fifth map ({ text, why }, placed at fifthAt(id)); Section II is three FRQs in the order no stimulus, one, two, from different units. Checked by checkForms (scripts/lib/aphug-exams.mjs).

hug-views-of-the-world-7.text: Places with the same number of people per square kilometer
hug-views-of-the-world-7.why: Lines of equal population density would need population data; this map's values are heights in meters.

hug-views-of-the-world-8.text: Along the South Coast, where the 100 meter line meets the sea
hug-views-of-the-world-8.why: The coast is the lowest, flattest land; steep land shows where the lines crowd together.

hug-views-of-the-world-9.text: The east, above 1,000 meters, where the lines are far apart
hug-views-of-the-world-9.why: Land above 1,000 meters lies in the west, by the Western Uplands; a port needs low, flat land on the coast.

hug-forced-voluntary-migration-3.text: Chain migration to join relatives in the city
hug-forced-voluntary-migration-3.why: Chain migration is Path 2, where a brother and cousins follow the first migrant; this first step of Path 1 is a move from a village to a city inside Mexico.

hug-forced-voluntary-migration-4.text: It leaves out the years in which the Path 2 migrants moved
hug-forced-voluntary-migration-4.why: The map gives the years for Path 2 (1995, 2001, 2008). What it cannot show is why anyone moved.

hug-transition-model-5.text: Country R and Country T equally
hug-transition-model-5.why: R, with high births and low deaths, fits stage 2; T, with low and close rates, fits stage 4. Stage 3 is falling births with low deaths, as in S.

hug-transition-model-6.text: Stage 1 is defined by migration, not by births and deaths
hug-transition-model-6.why: The model's stages are set by birth and death rates; migration is not part of it.

hug-transition-model-7.text: Reemergence of infectious and parasitic diseases
hug-transition-model-7.why: In that stage infections come back as leading killers; Country T’s leading causes are heart disease, cancer and stroke.

hug-diffusion-types-5.text: Expansion diffusion from Cherokee towns to English towns
hug-diffusion-types-5.why: The idea spread from English speakers to Sequoyah, not from Cherokee towns outward, and it was reworked on the way.

hug-diffusion-types-6.text: Many Cherokee people learned to read within a few years
hug-diffusion-types-6.why: Fast learning shows how quickly it spread, not that the trait changed as it spread.

hug-diffusion-types-7.text: Reverse hierarchical diffusion, from small villages up to cities
hug-diffusion-types-7.why: The passage describes learning from relatives and neighbors, person to person, with no order of places by size.

hug-defining-boundaries-4.why: Mark C is on the line between Kenya and Tanzania near Kilimanjaro: mostly straight geometric segments, not the crest of a range.

hug-defining-boundaries-5.why: The line follows a parallel of latitude, not a river or ridge, and it was drawn before most settlers arrived, so it is geometric and antecedent.

hug-von-thunen-5.text: Wheat, dairy and wood lots, from nearest to farthest
hug-von-thunen-5.why: In the table dairy is nearest (6 km) and wheat farther out (40 km); this order reverses them.

hug-von-thunen-6.text: Flowers grow better in the colder climate of the outer rings
hug-von-thunen-6.why: The table gives no climate for each ring; the reason in the table is how the flowers travel: refrigerated trucks and air freight.

hug-von-thunen-7.text: The number of tractors sold in Country A each year
hug-von-thunen-7.why: Tractor sales say little about where each farm type sits; the model's isolated state assumes flat, even land, so soil, slope and rivers are the test.

hug-cities-globalization-5.text: The factory workers live near the factory they work in
hug-cities-globalization-5.why: Living near work is distance at the local scale; time-space compression is about far places linked in less time.

hug-cities-globalization-6.text: Each world city makes its own decisions with no tie to others
hug-cities-globalization-6.why: The passage shows decisions in linked cities shaping distant work, so the cities are connected, not apart.

hug-cities-globalization-7.text: Local weather and the national price of phones
hug-cities-globalization-7.why: The passage says nothing about weather; it ties decisions made in world cities, at the global scale, to work in one place, the local scale.

hug-views-of-the-world-13.text: Absolute location: the latitude and longitude of the region
hug-views-of-the-world-13.why: Absolute location is a position on the grid; "Middle East" names a direction seen from Europe.

hug-data-sources-9.text: It replaces maps, so planners can stop using them
hug-data-sources-9.why: Satellite images are often turned into maps; remote sensing fits because it measures a huge, remote forest the same way each year.

hug-population-distribution-11.text: A physical factor: the inland plateau had more ports
hug-population-distribution-11.why: An inland plateau has no seaports; the move came from a government choice, a human factor.

hug-distribution-consequences-10.text: Egypt counts its desert as farmland in its arable totals
hug-distribution-consequences-10.why: Arable land is land that can grow crops; the desert is left out, which is why the farmland figure is small.

hug-culture-intro-10.text: Culture spreads to a person through the food she eats as a baby
hug-culture-intro-10.why: Food is one trait among many; her story shows that she learned language, sport and food from the people who raised her.

hug-culture-on-the-land-11.text: Separate entrances are a folk tradition found in each country
hug-culture-on-the-land-11.why: The example is one country's rules about gender and space, and the 2019 change shows the rules were cultural and could change.

hug-cultural-patterns-10.text: Tanzania's many languages became one creole by the 1970s
hug-cultural-patterns-10.why: Swahili was promoted alongside home languages; the many languages did not merge into one creole.

hug-diffusion-types-11.text: Stimulus diffusion, because neighbors change the bean into rice
hug-diffusion-types-11.why: The neighbors grow the same bean; stimulus diffusion would mean the idea is changed into something new.

hug-diffusion-history-9.text: Language extinction: the trade language replaced the others
hug-diffusion-history-9.why: Papua New Guinea still has hundreds of languages; Tok Pisin gaining native speakers is creolization.

hug-diffusion-today-10.text: Globalization makes English the first language of each country
hug-diffusion-today-10.why: English is widely used as a shared second language; most countries keep their own first languages.

hug-political-intro-10.why: Greenland is not an independent state; Denmark handles its defense and foreign policy.

hug-political-processes-9.text: State N's devolution of power to State M
hug-political-processes-9.why: Devolution is a state handing power to its own regions; here one state's soldiers entered another without permission.

hug-power-territoriality-9.text: Global scale, because property laws exist worldwide
hug-power-territoriality-9.why: The fence marks one farmer's land, so the territory claimed is local, whatever laws exist elsewhere.

hug-defining-boundaries-11.why: A superimposed boundary is forced on a landscape by an outside power and still works as a boundary; the wall pieces no longer divide anything.

hug-boundary-functions-11.why: A territorial sea is the 12 nautical miles off a coast; this strip is on land, with armed forces kept out.

hug-internal-boundaries-10.why: Gaining and losing seats after the census is reapportionment; drawing new lines afterward is redistricting.

hug-forms-of-governance-9.why: In a confederation the regions hold most power; here Paris sets school content and the regions carry it out.

hug-agriculture-intro-10.text: Long, cold winters with a short growing season
hug-agriculture-intro-10.why: Olives and citrus are damaged by long hard frosts; all three places have mild, rainy winters and hot, dry summers.

hug-settlement-survey-10.text: The government divided the land into large square sections for single farms
hug-settlement-survey-10.why: Square sections for single families spread farmhouses out; clustered villages come from sharing wells, defense and services.

hug-agricultural-origins-9.text: Factories in towns offered steady wages to farm families
hug-agricultural-origins-9.why: Factories came with the Industrial Revolution, thousands of years after farming began.

hug-second-agricultural-revolution-9.text: It was harvested by the new steam-powered machines
hug-second-agricultural-revolution-9.why: Steam machines came later; clover was grown to feed animals and to put nitrogen back into the soil.

hug-green-revolution-9.text: It grows best on poor soil with little water
hug-green-revolution-9.why: High-yield varieties give their large harvests when given water and fertilizer, which is why irrigation spread with them.

hug-urbanization-origins-11.text: Gold was found in the hills around the town
hug-urbanization-origins-11.why: Chicago grew as a transport hub where rail met lake shipping, not from a gold rush.

hug-cities-worldwide-11.text: A boomburb inside the central city
hug-cities-worldwide-11.why: A boomburb is a fast-growing suburb, and the family lives far outside the built-up metro area, among farms.

hug-cities-globalization-10.text: Stimulus diffusion as each town invents its own payment system
hug-cities-globalization-10.why: The same service spreads, and it moves from the largest cities down to small towns.

hug-city-size-distribution-12.text: Towns in the region have grown closer together
hug-city-size-distribution-12.why: Closer towns still fit the theory's idea of market areas; it is online shopping that removes many trips to a central place.

hug-industrial-revolution-10.text: Colonies in Africa and Asia had the newest factory machines
hug-industrial-revolution-10.why: The machines and factories were in Europe; colonies supplied raw materials and bought factory goods.

hug-economic-sectors-11.text: Factories moved inland because ports closed to container ships
hug-economic-sectors-11.why: Ports grew with container ships; cheaper shipping let factories sit far from their buyers.

hug-development-measures-11.why: The formal sector is registered and taxed; unregistered cash work from street stalls is informal.

hug-women-development-10.text: Factory work ended the gap between women's and men's wages
hug-women-development-10.why: Wages stayed low and a gap remained; the answer with both sides names income and the low pay and safety risks.

hug-development-theories-13.text: It leaves out the stage of mass consumption
hug-development-theories-13.why: Rostow's last stage is the age of high mass consumption, so the model includes it.

hug-trade-world-economy-9.text: A trade bloc that Costa Rica and Canada both belong to
hug-trade-world-economy-9.why: No shared bloc is needed to show the idea; each country supplies what the other needs, which is complementarity.

hug-world-economy-changes-13.text: Outsourcing of parts to other countries
hug-world-economy-changes-13.why: Outsourcing is about who makes the parts; delivering them hours before use is just-in-time.

hug-data-sources-5.why: A census counts people by asking them; these data were measured by satellite from far above.

hug-data-sources-6.text: Spread in a line along the eastern border, with few in the center
hug-data-sources-6.why: The lights cluster in the Capital Region and on the South Coast, not along one border.

hug-data-sources-7.text: Lights are counted by province, so the map hides the capital
hug-data-sources-7.why: The dots are placed where the lights are; the caution is that light shows power use, so unlit villages are missed.

hug-population-composition-6.text: More men than women are counted in the 80 and over group
hug-population-composition-6.why: The pyramid shows the reverse: the female bar is longer at 80 and over.

hug-population-composition-7.text: Whether more people are aged 45 to 49 than 0 to 4
hug-population-composition-7.why: The pyramid shows both bars, so it can answer this; it cannot show where in Country Q older people live.

hug-migration-effects-7.text: Migration changes the borders of the town
hug-migration-effects-7.why: Migration changes who lives in the town, not its borders; the meeting shows debate over services and visas.

hug-migration-effects-8.text: Most new workers in Riverton came from nearby farms
hug-migration-effects-8.why: Moves from nearby farms stay at the local scale; national visa rules link the town to the national scale.

hug-culture-on-the-land-6.text: The new glass tower beside the river
hug-culture-on-the-land-6.why: The tower is new in 2020; the brick mill and smokestack are left from the 1920 period.

hug-culture-on-the-land-7.text: Placelessness: the riverbank looks like any other place
hug-culture-on-the-land-7.why: Each period leaves a distinct mark that later groups reuse, so the panels show sequent occupance.

hug-centrifugal-centripetal-5.text: The Capital region has the least electricity
hug-centrifugal-centripetal-5.why: The Capital region has the most: 99% of homes. The Mareh-speaking Plateau and Desert have the least.

hug-centrifugal-centripetal-6.text: Language differences fade where electricity reaches homes
hug-centrifugal-centripetal-6.why: Nothing in the table shows language fading; poverty and language overlap, which can feed a sense of being left behind.

hug-centrifugal-centripetal-7.text: Which region has the highest income per person
hug-centrifugal-centripetal-7.why: The table gives income per person for each region, so it can answer this.

hug-agricultural-origins-5.why: The potato reached Ireland centuries before the Green Revolution, through the Columbian Exchange.

hug-agricultural-origins-6.text: Irish farmers grew many kinds of potato, so the blight had many targets
hug-agricultural-origins-6.why: Families depended on one kind, which is why one disease could ruin most of the food supply.

hug-agricultural-origins-7.text: A form of step migration inside Ireland
hug-agricultural-origins-7.why: Leaving Ireland is international migration, and the famine pushed people out: a push factor.

hug-city-size-distribution-5.text: Two equal cities, one in the north and one in the south
hug-city-size-distribution-5.why: The map shows one city far larger than the rest, in the Capital Region.

hug-city-size-distribution-6.text: The Northern Hills city and the Western Uplands city
hug-city-size-distribution-6.why: Both are small (60,000 and 100,000 people), so the model expects little interaction; it favors large cities close together.

hug-city-size-distribution-7.text: It gives the distance between the cities in kilometers
hug-city-size-distribution-7.why: Distances can be measured from a map; the limit is that it shows no flows of people or goods to test against.

hug-economic-sectors-5.text: 1970 and 2020, at both ends of the chart
hug-economic-sectors-5.why: The secondary share is 15% in 1970 and 21% in 2020, below its 30% peak in 1990 and 2000.

hug-economic-sectors-6.text: Services gave way to factories, then to farm work
hug-economic-sectors-6.why: The chart runs the other way: primary work fell, secondary rose then fell, and services grew.

hug-economic-sectors-8.text: Farm prices rose so high that people stopped buying food
hug-economic-sectors-8.why: Rising food prices would not cut farm jobs this way; machines let fewer farmers grow the food.

hug-views-of-the-world-16.why: Iowa's farmhouses are scattered evenly across the plains, which is dispersal.

hug-data-in-decisions-11.text: Flood maps are useful at the global scale alone
hug-data-in-decisions-11.why: A flood map for one house is local data, used here for a family decision.

hug-population-distribution-16.text: Most Australians live on farms spread across the interior
hug-population-distribution-16.why: Australia is highly urban, and its people cluster in east and southeast coastal cities.

hug-distribution-consequences-13.text: The hospital would have too many staff for so few homes
hug-distribution-consequences-13.why: Staffing is a planning choice; the problem low density causes is the long distance patients travel.

hug-population-composition-11.text: As a narrow band at ages 0 to 4
hug-population-composition-11.why: People born from 1946 to 1964 were 56 to 74 in 2020, so they form a wide band in late middle age.

hug-culture-intro-16.text: Folk culture leads nationally; popular culture survives locally
hug-culture-intro-16.why: This reverses the two scales: the national survey shows popular culture, and the province keeps a folk tradition.

hug-culture-on-the-land-14.text: A building style set by the dry climate of the Southwest
hug-culture-on-the-land-14.why: Climate alone does not explain the many sides or the east-facing door; those carry the beliefs of the Diné (Navajo) people.

hug-cultural-patterns-12.text: Language divides people at the local scale alone
hug-cultural-patterns-12.why: Catalan unites many people within Catalonia, while debates about the region divide Spain: one trait works differently at each scale.

hug-diffusion-types-13.text: Hierarchical diffusion: the style reached big cities first
hug-diffusion-types-13.why: A style spreading by contagion goes to nearby places first, with no order of places by size.

hug-diffusion-history-12.text: Relocation diffusion by Chinese settlers in Europe in the 700s
hug-diffusion-history-12.why: Papermaking passed along trade routes through Central Asia and Southwest Asia, not by Chinese settlement in Europe.

hug-diffusion-today-13.text: It replaces their culture with Canadian folk culture
hug-diffusion-today-13.why: Weekly calls and Filipino shows keep ties to home; technology here helps them keep their culture.

hug-political-intro-12.text: Koreans are a stateless nation; Kurds have two states
hug-political-intro-12.why: It is the reverse: Koreans have two states on the peninsula, and Kurds have none.

hug-political-processes-12.text: Each colonial power redrew the borders after leaving
hug-political-processes-12.why: The 1964 agreement kept colonial-era borders in place; it did not redraw them.

hug-power-territoriality-12.text: Neocolonialism and colonialism are two names for direct rule
hug-power-territoriality-12.why: Neocolonialism is indirect control through money and influence, so the two are different.

hug-boundary-functions-13.text: Delimited is a natural boundary; demarcated is a geometric one
hug-boundary-functions-13.why: Natural and geometric are kinds of lines; delimiting and demarcating are steps in drawing and marking one.

hug-internal-boundaries-12.why: A city council's districts are inside one city: the local scale.

hug-agriculture-intro-13.text: Fruit and vegetables need the larger fields found near cities
hug-agriculture-intro-13.why: Land near cities is costly, so fields there are small; market gardens sit close because the produce spoils.

hug-settlement-survey-14.text: The farm is split into long lots that run back from the creek
hug-settlement-survey-14.why: Long lots are a different survey system; the problem here is a boundary tied to a tree and a creek that can change.

hug-agricultural-origins-14.text: Contagious diffusion by ship between Europe's large cities
hug-agricultural-origins-14.why: Farming moved over land, generation by generation, from place to place: expansion diffusion.

hug-second-agricultural-revolution-12.text: Small farmers gained the commons as private land
hug-second-agricultural-revolution-12.why: The commons were fenced into larger private farms, and many small farmers lost access to them.

hug-green-revolution-13.text: It showed that population cannot grow without new seeds
hug-green-revolution-13.why: Population grew before and during the Green Revolution; what it challenged was Malthus's claim that food cannot keep up.

hug-production-regions-10.text: The soybeans spoil before they reach a market
hug-production-regions-10.why: Dry soybeans store well; the risk of one crop is that one pest or price drop hits everything.

hug-urbanization-origins-13.text: A move of most factories from cities to rural villages
hug-urbanization-origins-13.why: Loosening the rules let rural people move to city jobs, raising the urban share.

hug-cities-globalization-12.text: A decision at the regional scale has no effect elsewhere
hug-cities-globalization-12.why: The London decision cut jobs in Dhaka, so it did have an effect, at the local scale.

hug-city-structure-11.why: The galactic model stresses edge cities ringing an old downtown; many separate specialized centers is multiple nuclei.

hug-density-land-use-11.text: Redevelopment of the city's oldest blocks into towers
hug-density-land-use-11.why: Detroit lost people and houses were torn down: decline, not redevelopment.

hug-infrastructure-11.text: Kenya's banks had branches in each village before 2007
hug-infrastructure-11.why: If banks had reached every village, M-Pesa would have filled little need; cell towers reached more people than banks did.

hug-industrial-revolution-16.text: India became the main supplier of steam engines to Britain
hug-industrial-revolution-16.why: Britain built the steam engines; India's hand weavers lost buyers to cheap mill cloth.

hug-economic-sectors-14.text: Periphery countries have fewer farms than core countries
hug-economic-sectors-14.why: Periphery countries often have more people in farming; machines and service jobs shrink the primary share in the core.

hug-development-measures-15.text: The HDI measures income alone in newer reports
hug-development-measures-15.why: The HDI combines health, education and income in every report; values are revised between reports.

hug-women-development-12.text: Iceland's wage gap closed as soon as it became wealthy
hug-women-development-12.why: Iceland passed a law in 2017 to enforce equal pay, which shows policy, not wealth alone, shapes opportunity.
